conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be your doctor during this admission. You're here for your 23rd cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your CNS lymphoma, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been feeling okay since my last treatment. No headaches or weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We’ll start by making sure your urine is alkaline before giving the methotrexate. That helps protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. They gave me something in the IV to do that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll use sodium bicarbonate in your IV fluids. The methotrexate will be given tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Last time I felt nauseated afterward. Is that expected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common. We’ll give you prochlorperazine if needed, and you can use the lorazepam you already take if nausea or anxiety comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. I’m a little nervous, but I trust the process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll monitor your labs closely, especially your kidney and liver function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the methotrexate level? You check that too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll check it daily until it drops low enough. Leucovorin rescue starts 24 hours after the infusion to protect your healthy cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I remember that helped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also keep an eye on your blood counts. Your hemoglobin was a bit low on admission, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s always been a little low. From the chemo, I think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common. We call it chemotherapy-induced anemia. But you’re not needing transfusions, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take iron at home, but my doctor said not to during admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. We avoid certain supplements during chemo. You’re on docusate and senna for constipation—still taking those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every day. My ulcerative colitis has been quiet lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep managing that the same way. Any asthma symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’ve been using my inhaler as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll continue your usual meds. I’ll see you tomorrow morning before the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re ready to start your methotrexate infusion. Urine pH is above 8, so we’re safe to proceed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready. How long will it take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About four hours. You’ll stay in the infusion center, and we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dose is the same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 13,760 mg total, based on your body surface area. It’s a high dose, but we’ve done this safely before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I trust you. Just hope the nausea isn’t too bad this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you prochlorperazine at the first sign. Let the nurse know right away if you feel sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You did really well—no reactions so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I feel okay now, but I know it might hit later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you hydrated and start leucovorin tomorrow at the same time as the infusion ended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’m starting to feel nauseated. Can I take something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, let’s give you prochlorperazine now. Also try sipping water or ginger tea if you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I hate throwing up—it makes me anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the lorazepam available. Try to rest. The nausea should improve in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level is 0.45, which is expected. We’ve started leucovorin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a safe level?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s high, but we expect that. It needs to drop below 0.1. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys? The creatinine was good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, creatinine is 0.5, even better than before. Your liver enzymes are a bit elevated but not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Nausea better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I even ate some toast and chicken.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. That means you’re recovering well. We’ll check your methotrexate level one more time tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your methotrexate level is now 0.03, which is very low. Safe for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Does that mean I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll go home on oral leucovorin for a few more doses and return in a month for your next cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my aspirin? I stopped it for the admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart it today. We held it because of bleeding risk, but it’s safe now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Keep taking your meds, watch for nausea, and call if anything changes. See you next month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we refilled your lorazepam prescription in case you need it for nausea or anxiety at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. I’ll keep it on hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your depression—how have you been feeling emotionally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I think. A bit anxious around treatments, but citalopram helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Don’t hesitate to talk to your psychiatrist if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I’ve got support at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Take care of yourself. We’ll see you in four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be ready. Thank you, Doctor.
